final_answer:
No, the trial court did not err (most likely). Limitation: every primary-source fetch was blocked by the network proxy, so the authority below is known only from search-result summaries and is NOT firewall-verified; treat the answer as provisional.

Governing rule: Texas disqualification of a law firm over a side-switching nonlawyer (legal assistant/paralegal) follows a bright-line framework from Phoenix Founders v. Marshall (Tex. 1994) and In re American Home Products (Tex. 1998): a nonlawyer who worked on a matter for one side is conclusively presumed to have acquired confidences; the firm that later hires her is presumed to receive them unless it takes minimal prophylactic measures (admonishing/instructing the employee not to disclose and screening her from the matter). Where the nonlawyer worked on the same case for the opposing party, failure to take those measures requires disqualification. The Supreme Court of Texas decided In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026), on facts matching this question (2009 suit, Prestige Consulting, assistant's 13 occasions of limited secretarial work from 2017 to 2022, e-filing notices). Per the summary I could access, it held that (1) regardless of whether the nonlawyer was switching sides when hired, she must be admonished/screened before beginning work on a later-arising conflict for the employing firm, or the firm is disqualified, and (2) the opposing party's receipt of e-filing notifications does not conclusively establish waiver. It denied mandamus, leaving the disqualification order in place.

Application: Jones had worked for Apex on this very suit, with several hundred privileged communications and strategy meetings, so confidences are conclusively presumed acquired. Smith Fullingham did not inquire, admonish, or screen her at hire or before she worked on the case in 2017 to 2022; screening was announced only in January 2023, years after her work began. Her lack of recall and the firm's assertion that no confidences were shared do not rebut the presumption, and late screening does not cure. Her limited, secretarial role does not avoid the rule. Waiver: Apex acted within about two months of learning of her employment (Jan. to early March 2023); e-filing notices bearing her name do not conclusively show earlier knowledge or waiver. Disqualification was therefore proper.

Caveats: Zaidi's text was not read; the Phoenix Founders and American Home Products framework is from memory and unverified here. Standard of review is abuse of discretion via mandamus.
